idiom_name: sequence { yield } for synchronous staging; cold Flow for the asynchronous, cancellable form
implementation_notes: Kotlin's standard library turns staged evaluation into a construction: a sequence { } builder with yield suspends the producer until the consumer asks for the next element, and unlike an Iterable chain it builds no intermediate collections, so the expensive part is acquired one element at a time (kotlinlang notes that sequences perform all processing steps element by element and compute lazily when possible). Flow is the asynchronous twin: a cold flow's builder block does not run until a collector collects it, each collector triggers its own execution, and cancellation travels through the coroutine scope, which makes Flow the right carrier when the deferred part is remote and must be cancellable. close/use gives deterministic release of the stages that were acquired; a hand-written plan is still justified when collectors must share one expensive acquisition, because both Sequence and cold Flow re-execute per iteration or per collector unless shareIn/stateIn or an explicit cache is added.
pitfalls: A Sequence is not memoized: every terminal operation re-runs the whole pipeline, so a second traversal re-acquires the expensive parts and may observe different data unless the result is cached or shared.
Without a terminal operation nothing happens at all, so a staged resource that is built but never collected looks acquired and is not - a silent no-op in code that forgets to iterate.
A cold Flow runs per collector: two collectors mean two acquisitions of the expensive stage, and shareIn/stateIn is required before publishing one to many subscribers.

The flow builder must not emit from another coroutine context (kotlinlang documents that emit must not be called from a different context and withContext inside flow { } fails), so remote stages belong behind flowOn or channelFlow.
A partially consumed iterator holds the state it was reading from; an abandoned sequence iterator keeps whatever the builder opened unless it is closed explicitly.

variants.name: Cold Flow for asynchronous, cancellable staging
variants.idiom_name: flow { emit(...) } plus collect / buffered / flowOn
variants.implementation_notes: The asynchronous variant: flow { } describes how parts are produced and produces nothing until collected, emit() suspends instead of blocking, and collect() in a coroutine makes cancellation and back-pressure part of the stage. flowOn moves the producing stage to another dispatcher, so the expensive remote fetch does not run on the collector's thread, and operators like buffered/take bound how many parts are in flight. Choose it over Sequence whenever a stage can suspend or fail asynchronously; remember that each collector starts a fresh execution.
pitfalls: Each collection re-executes the whole flow, so a shared expensive stage needs shareIn/stateIn (or a cache) or every subscriber pays for it again.
Blocking calls inside flow { } occupy the producing coroutine; use flowOn(Dispatchers.IO) or a blocking-aware API instead of mixing blocking IO into the collector's context.
Cancelling the collecting job cancels the in-flight stage but does not undo parts already delivered, so the consumer must be prepared for a partially acquired resource.
